content: The manganate ion is represented as MnO₄²⁻, and a manganate compound is any chemical compound that contains the MnO₄²⁻ group. For example, potassium manganate is a manganate compound. Manganates are the conjugate bases of the hypothetical species manganic acid (H₂MnO₄), which is too unstable to be isolated. Manganate salts are intermediates in the industrial synthesis of potassium permanganate. It is important to note that manganate and permanganate salts are sometimes confused, but they exhibit significantly different chemical behaviors. The structure of the MnO₄²⁻ ion is tetrahedral, and it is structurally related to other tetrahedral oxides such as permanganate and osmium tetroxide. Salts of MnO₄²⁻, SO₄²⁻, and CrO₄²⁻ are typically isostructural or nearly so, meaning they form solid solutions and have similar solubility properties. However, unlike sulfate and chromate ions, MnO₄²⁻ is paramagnetic. The manganate ion is stable in aqueous solutions only under strongly basic conditions. Consequently, manganate salts are typically found with electropositive metals such as Na⁺, K⁺, and Ba²⁺, which do not form insoluble hydroxides. Manganates can be synthesized either by the oxidation of MnO₂ or by the reduction of permanganate. It is worth noting that molecular oxygen (O₂) is not a sufficiently strong oxidizing agent to convert Mn(VI) to Mn(VII). Therefore, the Mn(VI)/Mn(VII) oxidation requires stronger oxidants such as ozone (O₃) or chlorine (Cl₂). The manganate ion (MnO₄²⁻) is the conjugate base of the hypothetical manganic acid (H₂MnO₄), which is too unstable to isolate. However, the half-deprotonated form of the acid has been studied. The manganate ion is approximately 100 times more basic than the acetate ion. At lower pH levels, the manganate ion undergoes disproportionation to form permanganate (MnO₄⁻) and manganese dioxide (MnO₂). The chemical relationship between permanganate and manganate ions illustrates the close connection between these two principal soluble manganese oxides. Additionally, two rarer members of this series are known. Hypomanganate (MnO₄³⁻) is a blue-colored ion of Mn(V) that forms when MnO₄²⁻ is treated with manganite (MnO₄⁴⁻) at pH > 12. Hypomanganate can also be generated by treating KMnO₄ in 10 M KOH with H₂O₂, indicating that solutions of hypomanganate contain significant amounts of the protonated form even at high pH levels. Oxidation of alkenes by permanganate is proposed to proceed via intermediates involving esters of hypomanganate, such as MnO₂(OR)₂⁻, where R is an alkyl group. The brown-colored manganite ion, a Mn(IV) species, is produced by dissolving its parent acid anhydride (MnO₂) in strong alkali. Alternatively, MnO₄⁴⁻ can be generated by the reduction of MnO₄³⁻. Manganate salts such as BaMnO₄ and K₂MnO₄ are used as oxidizing agents for primary and secondary alcohols. Primary alcohols are oxidized to aldehydes and subsequently to carboxylic acids, while secondary alcohols are oxidized to ketones. Tertiary alcohols, however, cannot be oxidized in this manner. The use of manganates is similar to that of the Jones reagent in organic synthesis.
